writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene IV,” how does Shakespeare show wedding preparations? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene IV, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of wedding preparations? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene IV develops the idea of wedding preparations. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene IV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of wedding preparations. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene IV suggests about wedding preparations. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses irony in Act IV, Scene IV to complicate the reader's understanding of wedding preparations. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of wedding preparations responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene IV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of wedding preparations follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene IV and its treatment of wedding preparations. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene IV as evidence for a larger claim about wedding preparations in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene IV as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of wedding preparations. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “you to bed; faith, You’ll be sick to-morrow / For this night’s watching” (Act IV, Scene IV, Nurse (speech 4)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: you to bed; faith, You’ll be sick to-morrow / For this night’s watching

symbolsAndMotifs.name: haste and time
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Everything happens too fast: a four-day action, a marriage the day after meeting, a wedding moved up a day; Friar Laurence warns "they stumble that run fast." In this scene: “cot-quean, go, / Get you to bed; faith, You’ll be sick to-morrow / For this night’s watching” (Act IV, Scene IV, Nurse (speech 4)).

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
